items.context: Scuttles out when the kitchen light goes on.

img.author: CDC
img.alt: A small, flat, light brown insect with long antennae and spiny legs.

items.why: A German cockroach: flat body, long antennae and spiny legs built for speed.
items.pearl: A cockroach can live for about a week without its head. It finally dies of thirst.

items.context: Found on a gravel path in the desert at night.

img.author: CDC/ Mr. Graham Heid (cropped)
img.alt: A pale yellow creature with pincers and a curled tail on gravel.

items.why: A desert scorpion: grasping pincers and a tail ending in a stinger.
items.pearl: Scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light, which is how people find them at night.

items.context: Spotted under pine trees after autumn rain.

img.author: CDC/ James M. Stewart
img.alt: Several round caps with white spots on a reddish surface, on short white stalks.

items.why: The red-capped, white-spotted fly agaric, the classic fairy-tale toadstool.
items.pearl: It isn't native to Australia: it arrived with pine trees and now pops up in pine plantations. It's poisonous, so look but don't eat.

img.author: CDC
img.alt: A dark, flat, tightly coiled shell with a soft body peeking out beneath.

items.why: A freshwater ramshorn snail with its flat, coiled shell.
items.pearl: Most snails have blue blood, but ramshorn snails carry haemoglobin like us, so their blood is red.

items.context: Watching you from a bare winter tree.

img.author: CDC (cropped)
img.alt: A bird with big round eyes, ear-like tufts and streaky brown feathers among branches.

items.why: A great horned owl, with feather tufts and huge forward-facing eyes.
items.pearl: Those 'horns' are just feathers. Owls can't move their eyes, so they turn their heads up to about 270 degrees.

img.author: CDC/ James Gathany
img.alt: A stout insect with red eyes, an orange-patterned body and clear veined wings, on black.

items.why: A cicada: wide head, red eyes and clear, veined wings folded like a roof.
items.pearl: Male cicadas sing by rapidly buckling drum-like plates called tymbals on their sides.

items.context: Found in an old bag of flour.

img.author: CDC/ Margaret A. Parsons
img.alt: Two small dark brown beetles and three pale segmented larvae on a sandy-coloured surface.

items.why: Confused flour beetles and their larvae, common pantry pests.
items.pearl: The 'confused' flour beetle got its name because it's so often confused with its cousin, the red flour beetle.

items.context: Electron microscope view, about 12 times life size.

img.author: CDC/ Janice Haney Carr (cropped)
img.alt: A grey electron microscope image of a small insect tangled in fine strands.

items.why: An ant caught in sticky spider silk, seen under an electron microscope.
items.pearl: Weight for weight, some spider silk is as strong as steel and far stretchier.

items.context: Spotted on a leaf in late summer. Don't touch.

img.author: CDC/ Harold G. Scott (cropped)
img.alt: A short creature with spiky brown ends and a bright green middle with a brown oval patch.

items.why: A saddleback caterpillar, named for the green 'saddle cloth' with a brown 'seat'.
items.pearl: Its spines are hollow and deliver a sting that can hurt for hours.

items.context: Hiding in plain sight on a leaf.

img.author: CDC/ Dr. Frank Shaw (cropped)
img.alt: A brown, hairy, oddly shaped lump with curled arm-like flaps on a green leaf.

items.why: A hag moth caterpillar, whose fleshy curled flaps make it look like shed spider skin or leaf litter.
items.pearl: It's also called the monkey slug caterpillar. Birds tend to pass it by, thinking it isn't food.
